modelAnswer: The key points of Darwin's theory of natural selection are: (1) Overproduction - all living creatures are highly fertile, so their populations could grow quickly and produce large numbers of offspring. (2) Competition - because food supplies and other resources are limited, population sizes stay largely constant despite overproduction, creating competition for resources. (3) Variation - no two organisms are the same; individuals differ, they do not have equal chances of survival and reproduction, and much of this variation is heritable, passed on to offspring through genes. (4) Natural selection - only organisms that survive and reproduce give rise to the next generation, and only those with favourable (advantageous) variations tend to survive to reproductive age; over many generations, the population accumulates more advantageous genetic variations and fewer harmful ones, since natural selection is essentially a process of elimination in which only the fittest survive.

modelAnswer: Selection can drive evolution because whenever variants differ in survival or reproduction, the better-adapted ones leave more offspring and their traits rise in frequency generation after generation. Assessment shows it works wherever tested: peppered moths shifted colour with polluted bark, antibiotic-resistant bacteria spread under drug pressure, and farmers reshaped crops by choosing seed stock. Selection needs only variation, heredity and differential success, all three of which nature supplies constantly, so it remains a proven means of evolutionary change.

keyPoints: ["Comparative anatomy: evidence via homologous structures and vestigial structures.","Homologous structures: similar structure/arrangement in different species (e.g. limb bones), despite different functions, points to a shared ancestor.","Vestigial structures: reduced, largely non-functional remnants of structures that were useful in an ancestor, showing descent with modification."]
modelAnswer: Comparative anatomy is one of the pieces of evidence for evolution, and it works through homologous structures and vestigial structures. Homologous structures are body parts in different species that have a similar underlying structure and arrangement (for example the bones of a bat's wing, a human arm, and a whale's flipper), even though the organisms use them for very different purposes; this similarity is best explained by the different species having descended from a common ancestor and then adapting the same basic structure to different needs over time. Vestigial structures are reduced, seemingly non-functional body parts (structures that were functional in an ancestor) that are still present in a species; their presence is evidence that the species evolved from an ancestor in which the structure had a purpose, and evolution has since reduced its usefulness. Together, these anatomical similarities and leftover structures across species are strong evidence that different organisms share a common evolutionary origin.

keyPoints: ["Palaeontology = study of fossils (the fossil record).","Fossils in rock layers can be ordered chronologically by the age of the layer.","The record shows gradual change in traits over time, including transitional forms.","This gradual, ordered change is evidence that species descended with modification from earlier ancestors."]
modelAnswer: Palaeontology, the study of fossils, provides evidence for evolution through the fossil record. Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of organisms that lived in the past, and when they are found in successive layers of rock they can be arranged in the chronological order in which the rock layers were laid down. This ordered fossil record shows a gradual change in the traits of related organisms over long spans of time, with older rock layers generally containing simpler or more primitive forms and younger layers showing forms progressively more similar to species alive today, including transitional fossils that share features of two different groups. This gradual, layered pattern of change captured in the fossil record is strong evidence that today's species descended, with modification, from earlier ancestral forms, which is the central claim of evolution.
